# car-reason

Code reasoning engine for [Common Agent Runtime](https://github.com/Parslee-ai/car). Adaptive, graph-driven, learning.

## What it does

Instead of a hardcoded "diagnose → suggest → explain" pipeline, reasoning actions are **skills in the memgine graph**. The graph's spreading activation and success/failure tracking determine which actions to run, in what order, routed to which models. As outcomes accumulate, the routing improves without code changes.

## Usage

```
use ;
use ReasoningSession;
let inference = new;
let mut memgine = new;
// Seed the default reasoning skills
seed_defaults;
let memgine = new;
let session = new;
let result = session.reason.await?;
println!;
for s in &result.suggestions
println!;
```
## Where it fits

A higher-level capability over `car-memgine` + `car-inference` + `car-ast`. Used by the `car` CLI's diagnostic / fix slash commands and by `.claude-plugin/agents/reason.md`.

## Inference handle abstraction (Parslee-ai/car#189)

`ReasoningSession` does not depend on the concrete `InferenceEngine`. It holds an `Arc<dyn ReasoningInferenceHandle>` — the narrow trait surface this crate exports in [ handle.rs](https://docs.rs/src/handle.rs).

The trait extends [ car_inference::InferenceHandle](https://docs.rs/car-inference/src/handle.rs) (which provides

`generate` + `embed`) with three reasoning-specific methods:| Method | Used for | In-process impl | Daemon impl |
|---|---|---|---|
| `generate_tracked(req)` | Per-action `InferenceResult`(trace_id, model_used, latency_ms) | `InferenceEngine::generate_tracked` | daemon's `infer`JSON-RPC method |
| `find_model_by_name(name)` | Tier-picker checks whether a candidate model is registered before naming it | `unified_registry.find_by_name` | cached `models.list_unified`snapshot |
| `record_inferred_outcomes(action_results)` | Post-session learning loop (writes inferred outcomes for each action's trace) | takes the engine's tracker write lock | best-effort no-op (no `outcomes.resolve_pending`endpoint yet — follow-up) |

This lets callers pick the inference backend at runtime:

```
// In-process (offline dev, tests, CI)
let inference:  =
    new;
// Daemon-routed (`car-server` running locally; shared hot weights + accumulated profiles)
let inference:  =
    new;
```
`cmd_reason` in `car-cli` does the runtime selection — probes the daemon with a cheap `models.list` RPC and falls back to an embedded engine if unreachable. See `car-rs/crates/car-cli/src/daemon_handle.rs` for the daemon-side `ReasoningInferenceHandle` impl.

**Why a new trait instead of growing  InferenceHandle.**

`InferenceHandle` (added in #188 for memgine) is intentionally minimal — `generate` + `embed` — because memgine is reachable from many crates and a wide trait surface multiplies daemon-proxy work for every implementor. `ReasoningInferenceHandle` extends it with the three methods car-reason actually uses, keeping the lower-level trait clean while still letting daemon impls compose: `DaemonInferenceHandle` implements both, with one shared WebSocket connection.

# dingo_proto - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/dingo-proto/0.2.0/dingo_proto/

## Expand description

A high-performance, no_std-compatible DNS packet parser focused on speed and safety.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use dingo_proto::Message;
let packet = [
     // Header
     0x12, 0x34,             // ID = 0x1234
     0x01, 0x00,             // Flags: RD=1 (standard query with recursion desired)
     0x00, 0x01,             // QDCOUNT = 1
     0x00, 0x00,             // ANCOUNT = 0
     0x00, 0x00,             // NSCOUNT = 0
     0x00, 0x00,             // ARCOUNT = 0
     // Question section
     0x07, b'e', b'x', b'a', b'm', b'p', b'l', b'e',
     0x03, b'c', b'o', b'm',
     0x00,
     0x00, 0x01,             // QTYPE = A (1)
     0x00, 0x01,             // QCLASS = IN (1)
];
Message::parse(&packet).unwrap();
```

- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.Type.html)
- From section 3.2.2 of RFC 1035

# car-planner

Proposal scoring and search for [Common Agent Runtime](https://github.com/Parslee-ai/car).

## What it does

Sits between the model and `car-engine`: scores N candidate proposals using static verification + cost estimation, picks the best, and provides fallback ordering for replan scenarios.

Inspired by MARS (budget-aware MCTS) — uses `verify()` + `simulate()` as the evaluation function, **not LLM calls**. Pure Rust, zero inference cost.

## Usage

```
use ;
let planner = new;
let candidates = vec!;
let ranked = planner.rank;
let best = &ranked; // highest score first
```
## Where it fits

If you already have N candidate proposals, use this directly. If you also need CAR to *generate* the candidates via inference, use `car-active-planner`, which composes inference with this ranker. Exposed to FFI consumers as the standalone `rank_proposals` function.

# car-mcp 0.32.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/car-mcp/0.32.0

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

MCP (Model Context Protocol) server library — transport-agnostic dispatch for exposing CAR capabilities to MCP-aware clients.

Two transports use this crate today:

- **stdio**—- `car-mcp-server`binary, one client per process. Suitable for Claude Desktop / Cursor / Claude Code's- `--mcp-config`and any other client that follows the MCP spec's stdio framing. See [- `transport::stdio_loop`].
- **HTTP-streamable**—- `car-server`daemon endpoint, many concurrent clients sharing the same- `Runtime`/ policy chain / eventlog. Implemented in- `car-server-core`against the same [- `Server::handle`] entry point. (Phase 2 stage 4b — pending.)

Both share the same `Server::handle(Request) -> Option<Response>`
pure function, so transports stay separable from protocol logic.

## Why a library crate

Originally this lived in `car-mcp-server`'s `main.rs` as a
self-contained binary. v0.8 + the external-agent work made it
clear MCP needs to be a first-class daemon surface so every
external client (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, custom GPTs) gets
CAR's tools through the same governance layer. Extracting the
dispatch logic into a library lets the daemon embed it without
shelling out to a subprocess. See
`docs/proposals/external-agent-detection.md` (Phase 2 stage 4b).

# car-memgine

Graph-based memory engine for the [Common Agent Runtime](https://github.com/Parslee-ai/car).

## What it does

Memory is a graph. Nodes represent facts, skills, conversations, identity, and environment. Edges encode relationships: Supersedes, DependsOn, RelatedTo, Triggers, TemporalNext. Skills are learned procedures stored as graph nodes with trigger edges, matched via spreading activation, and tracked for success/failure. Supports distillation from event log traces.

## Usage

```
use ;
let engine = new;
engine.ingest_fact.await?;
let hits = engine.retrieve.await?;
```
## Crate features

- `metal`-- Apple Silicon GPU acceleration (via car-inference)
- `cuda`-- NVIDIA GPU acceleration (via car-inference)
- `ast`-- AST-aware skill representation via- `car-ast`

Part of [CAR](https://github.com/Parslee-ai/car) -- see the main repo for full documentation.

# wasmtime 46.0.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasmtime/46.0.1

A Bytecode Alliance project

## About

This crate is the Rust embedding API for the [Wasmtime](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime) project: a
cross-platform engine for running WebAssembly programs. Notable features of
Wasmtime are:

-
**Fast**. Wasmtime is built on the optimizing[Cranelift](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/blob/main/cranelift/README.md)code generator to quickly generate high-quality machine code either at runtime or ahead-of-time. Wasmtime's runtime is also optimized for cases such as efficient instantiation, low-overhead transitions between the embedder and wasm, and scalability of concurrent instances.
-
[Secure](https://docs.wasmtime.dev/security.html)[Google's OSS Fuzz](https://google.github.io/oss-fuzz/), leveraging Rust's API and runtime safety guarantees, careful design of features and APIs through an[RFC process](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/rfcs), a[security policy](https://bytecodealliance.org/security)in place for when things go wrong, and a[release policy](https://docs.wasmtime.dev/stability-release.html)for patching older versions as well. We follow best practices for defense-in-depth and known protections and mitigations for issues like Spectre. Finally, we're working to push the state-of-the-art by collaborating with academic researchers to formally verify critical parts of Wasmtime and Cranelift.
-
[Configurable](https://docs.rs/wasmtime/latest/wasmtime/struct.Config.html)
-
[WASI](https://docs.rs/wasmtime-wasi/latest/wasmtime_wasi/)[WASI standard](https://wasi.dev).
-
[Standards Compliant](https://docs.wasmtime.dev/stability-wasm-proposals.html)[official WebAssembly test suite](https://github.com/WebAssembly/testsuite), implements the[official C API of wasm](https://github.com/WebAssembly/wasm-c-api), and implements[future proposals to WebAssembly](https://github.com/WebAssembly/proposals)as well. Wasmtime developers are intimately engaged with the WebAssembly standards process all along the way too.

## Example

An example of using the Wasmtime embedding API for running a small WebAssembly module might look like:

```
use Result;
use *;
```
More examples and information can be found in the `wasmtime` crate's [online
documentation](https://docs.rs/wasmtime) as well.

## Documentation

The [wasmtime guide](https://bytecodealliance.github.io/wasmtime) is the best starting point to learn about what
Wasmtime can do for you or help answer your questions about Wasmtime. If you're
curious in contributing to Wasmtime, [it can also help you do
that](https://bytecodealliance.github.io/wasmtime/contributing.html)!

For information on supported versions of Wasmtime see [the corresponding online book
documentation](https://docs.wasmtime.dev/stability-release.html#current-versions).

# wasmtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasmtime/46.0.1/target-redirect/wasmtime/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#wasmtimes-embedding-api)Wasmtime’s embedding API

Wasmtime is a WebAssembly engine for JIT-compiled or ahead-of-time compiled
WebAssembly modules and components. More information about the Wasmtime
project as a whole can be found [in the documentation
book](https://docs.wasmtime.dev) whereas this documentation mostly focuses
on the API reference of the `wasmtime` crate itself.

This crate contains an API used to interact with [WebAssembly modules](https://webassembly.github.io/spec) or
[WebAssembly components](https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org). For example you can compile WebAssembly, create
instances, call functions, etc. As an embedder of WebAssembly you can also
provide guests functionality from the host by creating host-defined
functions, memories, globals, etc, which can do things that WebAssembly
cannot (such as print to the screen).

The `wasmtime` crate is designed to be safe, efficient, and ergonomic.
This enables executing WebAssembly without the embedder needing to use
`unsafe` code, meaning that you’re guaranteed there is no undefined behavior
or segfaults in either the WebAssembly guest or the host itself.

The `wasmtime` crate can roughly be thought of as being split into two
halves:

-
One half of the crate is similar to the [JS WebAssembly API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/WebAssembly)as well as the[proposed C API](https://github.com/webassembly/wasm-c-api)and is intended for working with[WebAssembly modules](https://webassembly.github.io/spec). This API resides in the root of the`wasmtime`crate’s namespace, for example`wasmtime::Module`
-
The second half of the crate is for use with the [WebAssembly Component Model](https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org). The implementation of the component model is present in`wasmtime::component``component::Func``Func`

An example of using Wasmtime to run a core WebAssembly module looks like:

```
use wasmtime::*;
fn main() -> wasmtime::Result<()> {
    let engine = Engine::default();
    // Modules can be compiled through either the text or binary format
    let wat = r#"
        (module
            (import "host" "host_func" (func $host_hello (param i32)))
            (func (export "hello")
                i32.const 3
                call $host_hello)
        )
    "#;
    let module = Module::new(&engine, wat)?;
    // Host functionality can be arbitrary Rust functions and is provided
    // to guests through a `Linker`.
    let mut linker = Linker::new(&engine);
    linker.func_wrap("host", "host_func", |caller: Caller<'_, u32>, param: i32| {
        println!("Got {} from WebAssembly", param);
        println!("my host state is: {}", caller.data());
    })?;
    // All wasm objects operate within the context of a "store". Each
    // `Store` has a type parameter to store host-specific data, which in
    // this case we're using `4` for.
    let mut store: Store<u32> = Store::new(&engine, 4);
    // Instantiation of a module requires specifying its imports and then
    // afterwards we can fetch exports by name, as well as asserting the
    // type signature of the function with `get_typed_func`.
    let instance = linker.instantiate(&mut store, &module)?;
    let hello = instance.get_typed_func::<(), ()>(&mut store, "hello")?;
    // And finally we can call the wasm!
    hello.call(&mut store, ())?;
    Ok(())
}
```

[§](https://docs.rs#async)Async

Wasmtime supports executing WebAssembly guests through Rust-level `async`
functions. This enables Wasmtime to block the guest without blocking the
host, interrupt infinite loops or long-running CPU-bound guests, and
integrate with Rust host functions that are themselves `async`.

Many functions in the embedding API have a sync variant and an async
variant, for example [ Func::call](https://docs.rs/struct.Func.html#method.call) and

[. Embedders may decide which is most appropriate for their use case, but if certain features of Wasmtime are configured then](https://docs.rs/struct.Func.html#method.call_async)

`Func::call_async``*_async` variants of functions are
required. If any of these features are used, for example, then `*_async`
must be used:- Async core wasm host functions, for example via `Linker::func_wrap_async`
- Async component host functions, for example via `component::LinkerInstance::func_wrap_async`
- Async resource limiters, via `Store::limiter_async`
- Async yields with fuel via `Store::fuel_async_yield_interval`
- Async yields via epochs via `Store::epoch_deadline_async_yield_and_update`

This is not an exhaustive list, but if any of these configurations/APIs are
used then all `*_async` APIs must be used in Wasmtime. If synchronous APIs
are used instead they will return an error.

[§](https://docs.rs#asynchronous-wasm)Asynchronous Wasm

Core WebAssembly and synchronous WIT functions (e.g. WASIp2-and-prior)
require that all imported functions appear synchronous from the perspective
of the guest. Host functions which perform I/O and block, however, are often
defined with `async` in Rust. Wasmtime’s async support bridges this gap with
asynchronous wasm execution.

When using `*_async` APIs to execute WebAssembly Wasmtime will always
represent its computation as a [ Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html). The

`poll` method of the futures
returned by Wasmtime will perform the actual work of calling the
WebAssembly. Wasmtime won’t manage its own thread pools or similar, that’s
left up to the embedder.To implement futures in a way that WebAssembly sees asynchronous host
functions as synchronous, all async Wasmtime futures will execute on a
separately allocated native stack from the thread otherwise executing
Wasmtime. This separate native stack can then be switched to and from.
Using this whenever an `async` host function returns a future that
resolves to `Pending` we switch away from the temporary stack back to
the main stack and propagate the `Pending` status.

[§](https://docs.rs#execution-in-poll)Execution in `poll`

The [ Future::poll](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html#tymethod.poll) method is the main driving force behind Rust’s futures.
That method’s own documentation states “an implementation of

`poll` should
strive to return quickly, and should not block”. This, however, can be at
odds with executing WebAssembly code as part of the `poll` method itself. If
your WebAssembly is untrusted then this could allow the `poll` method to
take arbitrarily long in the worst case, likely blocking all other
asynchronous tasks.To remedy this situation you have a few possible ways to solve this:

-
The most efficient solution is to enable `Config::epoch_interruption``crate::Store::epoch_deadline_async_yield_and_update``crate::Engine::increment_epoch``Future::poll`Note that to prevent infinite execution of wasm it’s recommended to place a timeout on the entire future representing executing wasm code and the periodic yields with epochs should ensure that when the timeout is reached it’s appropriately recognized.
-
Alternatively you can enable the `Config::consume_fuel``crate::Store::fuel_async_yield_interval``Poll::Pending`from their`poll`method, and will get automatically re-polled later. This enables the`Future::poll`method to take roughly a fixed amount of time since fuel is guaranteed to get consumed while wasm is executing. Unlike epoch-based preemption this is deterministic since wasm always consumes a fixed amount of fuel per-operation. The downside of this approach, however, is that the compiled code instrumentation is significantly more expensive than epoch checks.Note that to prevent infinite execution of wasm it’s recommended to place a timeout on the entire future representing executing wasm code and the periodic yields with epochs should ensure that when the timeout is reached it’s appropriately recognized.

In all cases special care needs to be taken when integrating asynchronous wasm into your application. You should carefully plan where WebAssembly will execute and what compute resources will be allotted to it. If Wasmtime doesn’t support exactly what you’d like just yet, please feel free to open an issue!

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate Features

The `wasmtime` crate comes with a number of compile-time features that can
be used to customize what features it supports. Some of these features are
just internal details, but some affect the public API of the `wasmtime`
crate. Wasmtime APIs gated behind a Cargo feature should be indicated as
such in the documentation.

-
`runtime`- Enabled by default, this feature enables executing WebAssembly modules and components. If a compiler is not available (such as`cranelift`) then`Module::deserialize`
-
`cranelift`- Enabled by default, this features enables using Cranelift at runtime to compile a WebAssembly module to native code. This feature is required to process and compile new WebAssembly modules and components.
-
`cache`- Enabled by default, this feature adds support for wasmtime to perform internal caching of modules in a global location. This must still be enabled explicitly through`Config::cache`
-
`wat`- Enabled by default, this feature adds support for accepting the text format of WebAssembly in`Module::new``Component::new`
-
`parallel-compilation`- Enabled by default, this feature enables support for compiling functions in parallel with`rayon`.
-
`async`- Enabled by default, this feature enables APIs and runtime support for defining asynchronous host functions and calling WebAssembly asynchronously. For more information see[async documentation](https://docs.rs#async)
-
`profiling`- Enabled by default, this feature compiles in support for profiling guest code via a number of possible strategies. See`Config::profiler`
-
`all-arch`- Not enabled by default. This feature compiles in support for all architectures for both the JIT compiler and the`wasmtime compile`CLI command. This can be combined with`Config::target`
-
`pooling-allocator`- Enabled by default, this feature adds support for`PoolingAllocationConfig``Config::allocation_strategy`
-
`demangle`- Enabled by default, this will affect how backtraces are printed and whether symbol names from WebAssembly are attempted to be demangled. Rust and C++ demanglings are currently supported.
-
`coredump`- Enabled by default, this will provide support for generating a core dump when a trap happens. This can be configured via`Config::coredump_on_trap`
-
`addr2line`- Enabled by default, this feature configures whether traps will attempt to parse DWARF debug information and convert WebAssembly addresses to source filenames and line numbers.
-
`debug-builtins`- Enabled by default, this feature includes some built-in debugging utilities and symbols for native debuggers such as GDB and LLDB to attach to the process Wasmtime is used within. The intrinsics provided will enable debugging guest code compiled to WebAssembly. This must also be enabled via`Config::debug_info`
-
`component-model`- Enabled by default, this enables support for the`wasmtime::component`
-
`gc`- Enabled by default, this enables support for a number of WebAssembly proposals such as`reference-types`,`function-references`, and`gc`. Note that the implementation of the`gc`proposal itself is not yet complete at this time.
-
`threads`- Enabled by default, this enables compile-time support for the WebAssembly`threads`proposal, notably shared memories.
-
`call-hook`- Disabled by default, this enables support for the`Store::call_hook`
-
`memory-protection-keys`- Disabled by default, this enables support for the`PoolingAllocationConfig::memory_protection_keys``call-hook`feature where entries/exits into WebAssembly will have more overhead than before.

More crate features can be found in the [manifest](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/blob/main/crates/wasmtime/Cargo.toml) of Wasmtime itself for
seeing what can be enabled and disabled.

# wasmtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime/46.0.1/wasmtime/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#wasmtimes-embedding-api)Wasmtime’s embedding API

Wasmtime is a WebAssembly engine for JIT-compiled or ahead-of-time compiled
WebAssembly modules and components. More information about the Wasmtime
project as a whole can be found [in the documentation
book](https://docs.wasmtime.dev) whereas this documentation mostly focuses
on the API reference of the `wasmtime` crate itself.

This crate contains an API used to interact with [WebAssembly modules](https://webassembly.github.io/spec) or
[WebAssembly components](https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org). For example you can compile WebAssembly, create
instances, call functions, etc. As an embedder of WebAssembly you can also
provide guests functionality from the host by creating host-defined
functions, memories, globals, etc, which can do things that WebAssembly
cannot (such as print to the screen).

The `wasmtime` crate is designed to be safe, efficient, and ergonomic.
This enables executing WebAssembly without the embedder needing to use
`unsafe` code, meaning that you’re guaranteed there is no undefined behavior
or segfaults in either the WebAssembly guest or the host itself.

The `wasmtime` crate can roughly be thought of as being split into two
halves:

-
One half of the crate is similar to the [JS WebAssembly API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/WebAssembly)as well as the[proposed C API](https://github.com/webassembly/wasm-c-api)and is intended for working with[WebAssembly modules](https://webassembly.github.io/spec). This API resides in the root of the`wasmtime`crate’s namespace, for example`wasmtime::Module`
-
The second half of the crate is for use with the [WebAssembly Component Model](https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org). The implementation of the component model is present in`wasmtime::component``component::Func``Func`

An example of using Wasmtime to run a core WebAssembly module looks like:

```
use wasmtime::*;
fn main() -> wasmtime::Result<()> {
    let engine = Engine::default();
    // Modules can be compiled through either the text or binary format
    let wat = r#"
        (module
            (import "host" "host_func" (func $host_hello (param i32)))
            (func (export "hello")
                i32.const 3
                call $host_hello)
        )
    "#;
    let module = Module::new(&engine, wat)?;
    // Host functionality can be arbitrary Rust functions and is provided
    // to guests through a `Linker`.
    let mut linker = Linker::new(&engine);
    linker.func_wrap("host", "host_func", |caller: Caller<'_, u32>, param: i32| {
        println!("Got {} from WebAssembly", param);
        println!("my host state is: {}", caller.data());
    })?;
    // All wasm objects operate within the context of a "store". Each
    // `Store` has a type parameter to store host-specific data, which in
    // this case we're using `4` for.
    let mut store: Store<u32> = Store::new(&engine, 4);
    // Instantiation of a module requires specifying its imports and then
    // afterwards we can fetch exports by name, as well as asserting the
    // type signature of the function with `get_typed_func`.
    let instance = linker.instantiate(&mut store, &module)?;
    let hello = instance.get_typed_func::<(), ()>(&mut store, "hello")?;
    // And finally we can call the wasm!
    hello.call(&mut store, ())?;
    Ok(())
}
```

[§](https://docs.rs#async)Async

Wasmtime supports executing WebAssembly guests through Rust-level `async`
functions. This enables Wasmtime to block the guest without blocking the
host, interrupt infinite loops or long-running CPU-bound guests, and
integrate with Rust host functions that are themselves `async`.

Many functions in the embedding API have a sync variant and an async
variant, for example [ Func::call](https://docs.rs/struct.Func.html#method.call) and

[. Embedders may decide which is most appropriate for their use case, but if certain features of Wasmtime are configured then](https://docs.rs/struct.Func.html#method.call_async)

`Func::call_async``*_async` variants of functions are
required. If any of these features are used, for example, then `*_async`
must be used:- Async core wasm host functions, for example via `Linker::func_wrap_async`
- Async component host functions, for example via `component::LinkerInstance::func_wrap_async`
- Async resource limiters, via `Store::limiter_async`
- Async yields with fuel via `Store::fuel_async_yield_interval`
- Async yields via epochs via `Store::epoch_deadline_async_yield_and_update`

This is not an exhaustive list, but if any of these configurations/APIs are
used then all `*_async` APIs must be used in Wasmtime. If synchronous APIs
are used instead they will return an error.

[§](https://docs.rs#asynchronous-wasm)Asynchronous Wasm

Core WebAssembly and synchronous WIT functions (e.g. WASIp2-and-prior)
require that all imported functions appear synchronous from the perspective
of the guest. Host functions which perform I/O and block, however, are often
defined with `async` in Rust. Wasmtime’s async support bridges this gap with
asynchronous wasm execution.

When using `*_async` APIs to execute WebAssembly Wasmtime will always
represent its computation as a [ Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html). The

`poll` method of the futures
returned by Wasmtime will perform the actual work of calling the
WebAssembly. Wasmtime won’t manage its own thread pools or similar, that’s
left up to the embedder.To implement futures in a way that WebAssembly sees asynchronous host
functions as synchronous, all async Wasmtime futures will execute on a
separately allocated native stack from the thread otherwise executing
Wasmtime. This separate native stack can then be switched to and from.
Using this whenever an `async` host function returns a future that
resolves to `Pending` we switch away from the temporary stack back to
the main stack and propagate the `Pending` status.

[§](https://docs.rs#execution-in-poll)Execution in `poll`

The [ Future::poll](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html#tymethod.poll) method is the main driving force behind Rust’s futures.
That method’s own documentation states “an implementation of

`poll` should
strive to return quickly, and should not block”. This, however, can be at
odds with executing WebAssembly code as part of the `poll` method itself. If
your WebAssembly is untrusted then this could allow the `poll` method to
take arbitrarily long in the worst case, likely blocking all other
asynchronous tasks.To remedy this situation you have a few possible ways to solve this:

-
The most efficient solution is to enable `Config::epoch_interruption``crate::Store::epoch_deadline_async_yield_and_update``crate::Engine::increment_epoch``Future::poll`Note that to prevent infinite execution of wasm it’s recommended to place a timeout on the entire future representing executing wasm code and the periodic yields with epochs should ensure that when the timeout is reached it’s appropriately recognized.
-
Alternatively you can enable the `Config::consume_fuel``crate::Store::fuel_async_yield_interval``Poll::Pending`from their`poll`method, and will get automatically re-polled later. This enables the`Future::poll`method to take roughly a fixed amount of time since fuel is guaranteed to get consumed while wasm is executing. Unlike epoch-based preemption this is deterministic since wasm always consumes a fixed amount of fuel per-operation. The downside of this approach, however, is that the compiled code instrumentation is significantly more expensive than epoch checks.Note that to prevent infinite execution of wasm it’s recommended to place a timeout on the entire future representing executing wasm code and the periodic yields with epochs should ensure that when the timeout is reached it’s appropriately recognized.

In all cases special care needs to be taken when integrating asynchronous wasm into your application. You should carefully plan where WebAssembly will execute and what compute resources will be allotted to it. If Wasmtime doesn’t support exactly what you’d like just yet, please feel free to open an issue!

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate Features

The `wasmtime` crate comes with a number of compile-time features that can
be used to customize what features it supports. Some of these features are
just internal details, but some affect the public API of the `wasmtime`
crate. Wasmtime APIs gated behind a Cargo feature should be indicated as
such in the documentation.

-
`runtime`- Enabled by default, this feature enables executing WebAssembly modules and components. If a compiler is not available (such as`cranelift`) then`Module::deserialize`
-
`cranelift`- Enabled by default, this features enables using Cranelift at runtime to compile a WebAssembly module to native code. This feature is required to process and compile new WebAssembly modules and components.
-
`cache`- Enabled by default, this feature adds support for wasmtime to perform internal caching of modules in a global location. This must still be enabled explicitly through`Config::cache`
-
`wat`- Enabled by default, this feature adds support for accepting the text format of WebAssembly in`Module::new``Component::new`
-
`parallel-compilation`- Enabled by default, this feature enables support for compiling functions in parallel with`rayon`.
-
`async`- Enabled by default, this feature enables APIs and runtime support for defining asynchronous host functions and calling WebAssembly asynchronously. For more information see[async documentation](https://docs.rs#async)
-
`profiling`- Enabled by default, this feature compiles in support for profiling guest code via a number of possible strategies. See`Config::profiler`
-
`all-arch`- Not enabled by default. This feature compiles in support for all architectures for both the JIT compiler and the`wasmtime compile`CLI command. This can be combined with`Config::target`
-
`pooling-allocator`- Enabled by default, this feature adds support for`PoolingAllocationConfig``Config::allocation_strategy`
-
`demangle`- Enabled by default, this will affect how backtraces are printed and whether symbol names from WebAssembly are attempted to be demangled. Rust and C++ demanglings are currently supported.
-
`coredump`- Enabled by default, this will provide support for generating a core dump when a trap happens. This can be configured via`Config::coredump_on_trap`
-
`addr2line`- Enabled by default, this feature configures whether traps will attempt to parse DWARF debug information and convert WebAssembly addresses to source filenames and line numbers.
-
`debug-builtins`- Enabled by default, this feature includes some built-in debugging utilities and symbols for native debuggers such as GDB and LLDB to attach to the process Wasmtime is used within. The intrinsics provided will enable debugging guest code compiled to WebAssembly. This must also be enabled via`Config::debug_info`
-
`component-model`- Enabled by default, this enables support for the`wasmtime::component`
-
`gc`- Enabled by default, this enables support for a number of WebAssembly proposals such as`reference-types`,`function-references`, and`gc`. Note that the implementation of the`gc`proposal itself is not yet complete at this time.
-
`threads`- Enabled by default, this enables compile-time support for the WebAssembly`threads`proposal, notably shared memories.
-
`call-hook`- Disabled by default, this enables support for the`Store::call_hook`
-
`memory-protection-keys`- Disabled by default, this enables support for the`PoolingAllocationConfig::memory_protection_keys``call-hook`feature where entries/exits into WebAssembly will have more overhead than before.

More crate features can be found in the [manifest](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/blob/main/crates/wasmtime/Cargo.toml) of Wasmtime itself for
seeing what can be enabled and disabled.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime/46.0.1/src/wasmtime/lib.rs.html

# wasmtime/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # Wasmtime's embedding API
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! Wasmtime is a WebAssembly engine for JIT-compiled or ahead-of-time compiled
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! WebAssembly modules and components. More information about the Wasmtime
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! project as a whole can be found [in the documentation
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! book](https://docs.wasmtime.dev) whereas this documentation mostly focuses
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! on the API reference of the `wasmtime` crate itself.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! This crate contains an API used to interact with [WebAssembly modules] or
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! [WebAssembly components]. For example you can compile WebAssembly, create
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! instances, call functions, etc. As an embedder of WebAssembly you can also
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! provide guests functionality from the host by creating host-defined
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! functions, memories, globals, etc, which can do things that WebAssembly
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! cannot (such as print to the screen).
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! [WebAssembly modules]: https://webassembly.github.io/spec
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! [WebAssembly components]: https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! The `wasmtime` crate is designed to be safe, efficient, and ergonomic.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! This enables executing WebAssembly without the embedder needing to use
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! `unsafe` code, meaning that you're guaranteed there is no undefined behavior
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! or segfaults in either the WebAssembly guest or the host itself.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! The `wasmtime` crate can roughly be thought of as being split into two
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! halves:
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! * One half of the crate is similar to the [JS WebAssembly
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!   API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/WebAssembly) as well as the
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!   [proposed C API](https://github.com/webassembly/wasm-c-api) and is
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!   intended for working with [WebAssembly modules]. This API resides in the
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!   root of the `wasmtime` crate's namespace, for example
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!   [`wasmtime::Module`](`Module`).
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! * The second half of the crate is for use with the [WebAssembly Component
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!   Model]. The implementation of the component model is present in
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!   [`wasmtime::component`](`component`) and roughly mirrors the structure for
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!   core WebAssembly, for example [`component::Func`] mirrors [`Func`].
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! [WebAssembly Component Model]: https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! An example of using Wasmtime to run a core WebAssembly module looks like:
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! ```
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! use wasmtime::*;
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! fn main() -> wasmtime::Result<()> {
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!     let engine = Engine::default();
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!     // Modules can be compiled through either the text or binary format
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!     let wat = r#"
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!         (module
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!             (import "host" "host_func" (func $host_hello (param i32)))
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!             (func (export "hello")
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!                 i32.const 3
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!                 call $host_hello)
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!         )
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!     "#;
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!     let module = Module::new(&engine, wat)?;
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!     // Host functionality can be arbitrary Rust functions and is provided
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!     // to guests through a `Linker`.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!     let mut linker = Linker::new(&engine);
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!     linker.func_wrap("host", "host_func", |caller: Caller<'_, u32>, param: i32| {
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!         println!("Got {} from WebAssembly", param);
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!         println!("my host state is: {}", caller.data());
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!     })?;
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!     // All wasm objects operate within the context of a "store". Each
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!     // `Store` has a type parameter to store host-specific data, which in
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!     // this case we're using `4` for.
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!     let mut store: Store<u32> = Store::new(&engine, 4);
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!     // Instantiation of a module requires specifying its imports and then
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!     // afterwards we can fetch exports by name, as well as asserting the
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!     // type signature of the function with `get_typed_func`.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!     let instance = linker.instantiate(&mut store, &module)?;
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!     let hello = instance.get_typed_func::<(), ()>(&mut store, "hello")?;
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!     // And finally we can call the wasm!
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!     hello.call(&mut store, ())?;
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!     Ok(())
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! }
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! ```
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! ## Core Concepts
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! There are a number of core types and concepts that are important to be aware
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! of when using the `wasmtime` crate:
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! * [`Engine`] - a global compilation and runtime environment for WebAssembly.
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!   An [`Engine`] is an object that can be shared concurrently across threads
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!   and is created with a [`Config`] with many knobs for configuring
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!   behavior. Compiling or executing any WebAssembly requires first
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!   configuring and creating an [`Engine`]. All [`Module`]s and
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//!   [`Component`](component::Component)s belong to an [`Engine`], and
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!   typically there's one [`Engine`] per process.
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! * [`Store`] - container for all information related to WebAssembly objects
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!   such as functions, instances, memories, etc. A [`Store<T>`][`Store`]
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!   allows customization of the `T` to store arbitrary host data within a
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!   [`Store`]. This host data can be accessed through host functions via the
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!   [`Caller`] function parameter in host-defined functions. A [`Store`] is
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!   required for all WebAssembly operations, such as calling a wasm function.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!   The [`Store`] is passed in as a "context" to methods like [`Func::call`].
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!   Dropping a [`Store`] will deallocate all memory associated with
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!   WebAssembly objects within the [`Store`]. A [`Store`] is cheap to create
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!   and destroy and does not GC objects such as unused instances internally,
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!   so it's intended to be short-lived (or no longer than the instances it
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!   contains).
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! * [`Linker`] (or [`component::Linker`]) - host functions are defined within
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!   a linker to provide them a string-based name which can be looked up when
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!   instantiating a WebAssembly module or component. Linkers are traditionally
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!   populated at startup and then reused for all future instantiations of all
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!   instances, assuming the set of host functions does not change over time.
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!   Host functions are `Fn(..) + Send + Sync` and typically do not close over
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!   mutable state. Instead it's recommended to store mutable state in the `T`
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!   of [`Store<T>`] which is accessed through [`Caller<'_,
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!   T>`](crate::Caller) provided to host functions.
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! * [`Module`] (or [`Component`](component::Component)) - a compiled
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!   WebAssembly module or component. These structures contain compiled
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!   executable code from a WebAssembly binary which is ready to execute after
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!   being instantiated. These are expensive to create as they require
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!   compilation of the input WebAssembly. Modules and components are safe to
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!   share across threads, however. Modules and components can additionally be
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!   [serialized into a list of bytes](crate::Module::serialize) to later be
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!   [deserialized](crate::Module::deserialize) quickly. This enables JIT-style
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!   compilation through constructors such as [`Module::new`] and AOT-style
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!   compilation by having the compilation process use [`Module::serialize`]
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!   and the execution process use [`Module::deserialize`].
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! * [`Instance`] (or [`component::Instance`]) - an instantiated WebAssembly
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!   module or component. An instance is where you can actually acquire a
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!   [`Func`] (or [`component::Func`]) from, for example, to call.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! * [`Func`] (or [`component::Func`]) - a WebAssembly function. This can be
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!   acquired as the export of an [`Instance`] to call WebAssembly functions,
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!   or it can be created via functions like [`Func::wrap`] to wrap
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!   host-defined functionality and give it to WebAssembly. Functions also have
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!   typed views as [`TypedFunc`] or [`component::TypedFunc`] for a more
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!   efficient calling convention.
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! * [`Table`], [`Global`], [`Memory`], [`component::Resource`] - other
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!   WebAssembly objects which can either be defined on the host or in wasm
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//!   itself (via instances). These all have various ways of being interacted
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!   with like [`Func`].
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! All "store-connected" types such as [`Func`], [`Memory`], etc, require the
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! store to be passed in as a context to each method. Methods in wasmtime
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! frequently have their first parameter as either [`impl
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! AsContext`][`AsContext`] or [`impl AsContextMut`][`AsContextMut`]. These
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! traits are implemented for a variety of types, allowing you to, for example,
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! pass the following types into methods:
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! * `&Store<T>`
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! * `&mut Store<T>`
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! * `&Caller<'_, T>`
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! * `&mut Caller<'_, T>`
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! * `StoreContext<'_, T>`
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! * `StoreContextMut<'_, T>`
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! A [`Store`] is the sole owner of all WebAssembly internals. Types like
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! [`Func`] point within the [`Store`] and require the [`Store`] to be provided
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! to actually access the internals of the WebAssembly function, for instance.
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! ## WASI
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//!
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! The `wasmtime` crate does not natively provide support for WASI, but you can
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! use the [`wasmtime-wasi`] crate for that purpose. With [`wasmtime-wasi`] all
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! WASI functions can be added to a [`Linker`] and then used to instantiate
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! WASI-using modules. For more information see the [WASI example in the
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! documentation](https://docs.wasmtime.dev/examples-rust-wasi.html).
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//!
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! [`wasmtime-wasi`]: https://crates.io/crates/wasmtime-wasi
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//!
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! ## Async
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//!
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! Wasmtime supports executing WebAssembly guests through Rust-level `async`
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! functions. This enables Wasmtime to block the guest without blocking the
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! host, interrupt infinite loops or long-running CPU-bound guests, and
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! integrate with Rust host functions that are themselves `async`.
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! Many functions in the embedding API have a sync variant and an async
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! variant, for example [`Func::call`] and [`Func::call_async`]. Embedders
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! may decide which is most appropriate for their use case, but if certain
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! features of Wasmtime are configured then `*_async` variants of functions are
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! required. If any of these features are used, for example, then `*_async`
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! must be used:
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! * Async core wasm host functions, for example via [`Linker::func_wrap_async`]
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! * Async component host functions, for example via [`component::LinkerInstance::func_wrap_async`]
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! * Async resource limiters, via [`Store::limiter_async`]
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! * Async yields with fuel via [`Store::fuel_async_yield_interval`]
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! * Async yields via epochs via [`Store::epoch_deadline_async_yield_and_update`]
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//!
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! This is not an exhaustive list, but if any of these configurations/APIs are
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! used then all `*_async` APIs must be used in Wasmtime. If synchronous APIs
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! are used instead they will return an error.
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! #### Asynchronous Wasm
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//!
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! Core WebAssembly and synchronous WIT functions (e.g. WASIp2-and-prior)
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! require that all imported functions appear synchronous from the perspective
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! of the guest. Host functions which perform I/O and block, however, are often
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! defined with `async` in Rust. Wasmtime's async support bridges this gap with
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! asynchronous wasm execution.
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! When using `*_async` APIs to execute WebAssembly Wasmtime will always
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! represent its computation as a [`Future`]. The `poll` method of the futures
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! returned by Wasmtime will perform the actual work of calling the
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! WebAssembly. Wasmtime won't manage its own thread pools or similar, that's
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! left up to the embedder.
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//!
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! To implement futures in a way that WebAssembly sees asynchronous host
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! functions as synchronous, all async Wasmtime futures will execute on a
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! separately allocated native stack from the thread otherwise executing
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! Wasmtime. This separate native stack can then be switched to and from.
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! Using this whenever an `async` host function returns a future that
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! resolves to `Pending` we switch away from the temporary stack back to
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! the main stack and propagate the `Pending` status.
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//!
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! #### Execution in `poll`
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//!
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! The [`Future::poll`] method is the main driving force behind Rust's futures.
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! That method's own documentation states "an implementation of `poll` should
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! strive to return quickly, and should not block". This, however, can be at
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! odds with executing WebAssembly code as part of the `poll` method itself. If
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! your WebAssembly is untrusted then this could allow the `poll` method to
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! take arbitrarily long in the worst case, likely blocking all other
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//! asynchronous tasks.
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//! To remedy this situation you have a few possible ways to solve this:
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//!
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! * The most efficient solution is to enable
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//!   [`Config::epoch_interruption`] in conjunction with
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!   [`crate::Store::epoch_deadline_async_yield_and_update`]. Coupled with
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!   periodic calls to [`crate::Engine::increment_epoch`] this will cause
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//!   executing WebAssembly to periodically yield back according to the
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//!   epoch configuration settings. This enables [`Future::poll`] to take at
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//!   most a certain amount of time according to epoch configuration
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!   settings and when increments happen. The benefit of this approach is
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//!   that the instrumentation in compiled code is quite lightweight, but a
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//!   downside can be that the scheduling is somewhat nondeterministic since
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//!   increments are usually timer-based which are not always deterministic.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//!
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!   Note that to prevent infinite execution of wasm it's recommended to
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//!   place a timeout on the entire future representing executing wasm code
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//!   and the periodic yields with epochs should ensure that when the
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//!   timeout is reached it's appropriately recognized.
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! * Alternatively you can enable the
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//!   [`Config::consume_fuel`](crate::Config::consume_fuel) method as well
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!   as [`crate::Store::fuel_async_yield_interval`] When doing so this will
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//!   configure Wasmtime futures to yield periodically while they're
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!   executing WebAssembly code. After consuming the specified amount of
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//!   fuel wasm futures will return `Poll::Pending` from their `poll`
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//!   method, and will get automatically re-polled later. This enables the
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//!   `Future::poll` method to take roughly a fixed amount of time since
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//!   fuel is guaranteed to get consumed while wasm is executing. Unlike
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!   epoch-based preemption this is deterministic since wasm always
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//!   consumes a fixed amount of fuel per-operation. The downside of this
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//!   approach, however, is that the compiled code instrumentation is
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//!   significantly more expensive than epoch checks.
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//!
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//!   Note that to prevent infinite execution of wasm it's recommended to
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//!   place a timeout on the entire future representing executing wasm code
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//!   and the periodic yields with epochs should ensure that when the
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//!   timeout is reached it's appropriately recognized.
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//!
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//! In all cases special care needs to be taken when integrating
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! asynchronous wasm into your application. You should carefully plan where
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! WebAssembly will execute and what compute resources will be allotted to
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! it. If Wasmtime doesn't support exactly what you'd like just yet, please
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! feel free to open an issue!
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//!
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//! ## Crate Features
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//!
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//! The `wasmtime` crate comes with a number of compile-time features that can
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! be used to customize what features it supports. Some of these features are
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! just internal details, but some affect the public API of the `wasmtime`
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//! crate. Wasmtime APIs gated behind a Cargo feature should be indicated as
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//! such in the documentation.
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//!
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//! * `runtime` - Enabled by default, this feature enables executing
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//!   WebAssembly modules and components. If a compiler is not available (such
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//!   as `cranelift`) then [`Module::deserialize`] must be used, for example, to
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//!   provide an ahead-of-time compiled artifact to execute WebAssembly.
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//!
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//! * `cranelift` - Enabled by default, this features enables using Cranelift at
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//!   runtime to compile a WebAssembly module to native code. This feature is
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//!   required to process and compile new WebAssembly modules and components.
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//!
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! * `cache` - Enabled by default, this feature adds support for wasmtime to
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//!   perform internal caching of modules in a global location. This must still
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//!   be enabled explicitly through [`Config::cache`].
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//!
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//! * `wat` - Enabled by default, this feature adds support for accepting the
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//!   text format of WebAssembly in [`Module::new`] and
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//!   [`Component::new`](component::Component::new). The text format will be
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//!   automatically recognized and translated to binary when compiling a
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//!   module.
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//!
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//! * `parallel-compilation` - Enabled by default, this feature enables support
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//!   for compiling functions in parallel with `rayon`.
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//!
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//! * `async` - Enabled by default, this feature enables APIs and runtime
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//!   support for defining asynchronous host functions and calling WebAssembly
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//!   asynchronously. For more information see [async documentation](#async)
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//!
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//! * `profiling` - Enabled by default, this feature compiles in support for
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//!   profiling guest code via a number of possible strategies. See
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//!   [`Config::profiler`] for more information.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//!
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//! * `all-arch` - Not enabled by default. This feature compiles in support for
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//!   all architectures for both the JIT compiler and the `wasmtime compile` CLI
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//!   command. This can be combined with [`Config::target`] to precompile
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//!   modules for a different platform than the host.
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//!
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//! * `pooling-allocator` - Enabled by default, this feature adds support for
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//!   [`PoolingAllocationConfig`] to pass to [`Config::allocation_strategy`].
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//!   The pooling allocator can enable efficient reuse of resources for
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//!   high-concurrency and high-instantiation-count scenarios.
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//!
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//! * `demangle` - Enabled by default, this will affect how backtraces are
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//!   printed and whether symbol names from WebAssembly are attempted to be
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!   demangled. Rust and C++ demanglings are currently supported.
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//!
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//! * `coredump` - Enabled by default, this will provide support for generating
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//!   a core dump when a trap happens. This can be configured via
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//!   [`Config::coredump_on_trap`].
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//!
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//! * `addr2line` - Enabled by default, this feature configures whether traps
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//!   will attempt to parse DWARF debug information and convert WebAssembly
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//!   addresses to source filenames and line numbers.
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//!
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//! * `debug-builtins` - Enabled by default, this feature includes some built-in
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//!   debugging utilities and symbols for native debuggers such as GDB and LLDB
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//!   to attach to the process Wasmtime is used within. The intrinsics provided
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//!   will enable debugging guest code compiled to WebAssembly. This must also
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//!   be enabled via [`Config::debug_info`] as well for guests.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//!
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//! * `component-model` - Enabled by default, this enables support for the
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//!   [`wasmtime::component`](component) API for working with components.
[347](https://docs.rs#347)//!
[348](https://docs.rs#348)//! * `gc` - Enabled by default, this enables support for a number of
[349](https://docs.rs#349)//!   WebAssembly proposals such as `reference-types`, `function-references`,
[350](https://docs.rs#350)//!   and `gc`. Note that the implementation of the `gc` proposal itself is not
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//!   yet complete at this time.
[352](https://docs.rs#352)//!
[353](https://docs.rs#353)//! * `threads` - Enabled by default, this enables compile-time support for the
[354](https://docs.rs#354)//!   WebAssembly `threads` proposal, notably shared memories.
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//!
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//! * `call-hook` - Disabled by default, this enables support for the
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//!   [`Store::call_hook`] API. This incurs a small overhead on all
[358](https://docs.rs#358)//!   entries/exits from WebAssembly and may want to be disabled by some
[359](https://docs.rs#359)//!   embedders.
[360](https://docs.rs#360)//!
[361](https://docs.rs#361)//! * `memory-protection-keys` - Disabled by default, this enables support for
[362](https://docs.rs#362)//!   the [`PoolingAllocationConfig::memory_protection_keys`] API. This feature
[363](https://docs.rs#363)//!   currently only works on x64 Linux and can enable compacting the virtual
[364](https://docs.rs#364)//!   memory allocation for linear memories in the pooling allocator. This comes
[365](https://docs.rs#365)//!   with the same overhead as the `call-hook` feature where entries/exits into
[366](https://docs.rs#366)//!   WebAssembly will have more overhead than before.
[367](https://docs.rs#367)//!
[368](https://docs.rs#368)//! More crate features can be found in the [manifest] of Wasmtime itself for
[369](https://docs.rs#369)//! seeing what can be enabled and disabled.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)//!
[371](https://docs.rs#371)//! [manifest]: https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/blob/main/crates/wasmtime/Cargo.toml

[420](https://docs.rs#420)/// A helper macro to safely map `MaybeUninit<T>` to `MaybeUninit<U>` where `U`
[421](https://docs.rs#421)/// is a field projection within `T`.
[422](https://docs.rs#422)///
[423](https://docs.rs#423)/// This is intended to be invoked as:
[424](https://docs.rs#424)///
[425](https://docs.rs#425)/// ```ignore
[426](https://docs.rs#426)/// struct MyType {
[427](https://docs.rs#427)///     field: u32,
[428](https://docs.rs#428)/// }
[429](https://docs.rs#429)///
[430](https://docs.rs#430)/// let initial: &mut MaybeUninit<MyType> = ...;
[431](https://docs.rs#431)/// let field: &mut MaybeUninit<u32> = map_maybe_uninit!(initial.field);
[432](https://docs.rs#432)/// ```
[433](https://docs.rs#433)///
[434](https://docs.rs#434)/// Note that array accesses are also supported:
[435](https://docs.rs#435)///
[436](https://docs.rs#436)/// ```ignore
[437](https://docs.rs#437)///
[438](https://docs.rs#438)/// let initial: &mut MaybeUninit<[u32; 2]> = ...;
[439](https://docs.rs#439)/// let element: &mut MaybeUninit<u32> = map_maybe_uninit!(initial[1]);
[440](https://docs.rs#440)/// ```
[441](https://docs.rs#441)#[doc(hidden)]
[442](https://docs.rs#442)#[macro_export]
[443](https://docs.rs#443)macro_rules! map_maybe_uninit {
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    ($maybe_uninit:ident $($field:tt)*) => ({
[445](https://docs.rs#445)        #[allow(unused_unsafe, reason = "macro-generated code")]
[446](https://docs.rs#446)        {
[447](https://docs.rs#447)            unsafe {
[448](https://docs.rs#448)                use $crate::MaybeUninitExt;
[449](https://docs.rs#449)
[450](https://docs.rs#450)                let m: &mut core::mem::MaybeUninit<_> = $maybe_uninit;
[451](https://docs.rs#451)                // Note the usage of `&raw` here which is an attempt to "stay
[452](https://docs.rs#452)                // safe" here where we never accidentally create `&mut T` where `T` is
[453](https://docs.rs#453)                // actually uninitialized, hopefully appeasing the Rust unsafe
[454](https://docs.rs#454)                // guidelines gods.
[455](https://docs.rs#455)                m.map(|p| &raw mut (*p)$($field)*)
[456](https://docs.rs#456)            }
[457](https://docs.rs#457)        }
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    })
[459](https://docs.rs#459)}
[460](https://docs.rs#460)
[461](https://docs.rs#461)#[doc(hidden)]
[462](https://docs.rs#462)pub trait MaybeUninitExt<T> {
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    /// Maps `MaybeUninit<T>` to `MaybeUninit<U>` using the closure provided.
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    ///
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    /// # Safety
[466](https://docs.rs#466)    ///
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    /// Requires that `*mut U` is a field projection from `*mut T`. Use
[468](https://docs.rs#468)    /// `map_maybe_uninit!` above instead.
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    unsafe fn map<U>(&mut self, f: impl FnOnce(*mut T) -> *mut U)
[470](https://docs.rs#470)    -> &mut core::mem::MaybeUninit<U>;
[471](https://docs.rs#471)}
[472](https://docs.rs#472)
[473](https://docs.rs#473)impl<T> MaybeUninitExt<T> for core::mem::MaybeUninit<T> {
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    unsafe fn map<U>(
[475](https://docs.rs#475)        &mut self,
[476](https://docs.rs#476)        f: impl FnOnce(*mut T) -> *mut U,
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    ) -> &mut core::mem::MaybeUninit<U> {
[478](https://docs.rs#478)        let new_ptr = f(self.as_mut_ptr());
[479](https://docs.rs#479)        // SAFETY: the memory layout of these two types are the same, and
[480](https://docs.rs#480)        // asserting that it's a safe reference with the same lifetime as `self`
[481](https://docs.rs#481)        // is a requirement of this function itself.
[482](https://docs.rs#482)        unsafe { core::mem::transmute::<*mut U, &mut core::mem::MaybeUninit<U>>(new_ptr) }
[483](https://docs.rs#483)    }

# Module in wasmtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasmtime/46.0.1/wasmtime/struct.Module.html

`pub struct Module { /* private fields */ }`**crate feature**only.

`runtime`## Expand description

A compiled WebAssembly module, ready to be instantiated.

A `Module` is a compiled in-memory representation of an input WebAssembly
binary. A `Module` is then used to create an [ Instance](https://docs.rs/struct.Instance.html)
through an instantiation process. You cannot call functions or fetch
globals, for example, on a

`Module` because it’s purely a code
representation. Instead you’ll need to create an
[to interact with the wasm module.](https://docs.rs/struct.Instance.html)

`Instance`A `Module` can be created by compiling WebAssembly code through APIs such as
[ Module::new](https://docs.rs/struct.Module.html#method.new). This would be a JIT-style use case where code is compiled
just before it’s used. Alternatively a

`Module` can be compiled in one
process and [can be used to save it to storage. A later call to](https://docs.rs/struct.Module.html#method.serialize)

`Module::serialize`[will quickly load the module to execute and does not need to compile any code, representing a more AOT-style use case.](https://docs.rs/struct.Module.html#method.deserialize)

`Module::deserialize`Currently a `Module` does not implement any form of tiering or dynamic
optimization of compiled code. Creation of a `Module` via [ Module::new](https://docs.rs/struct.Module.html#method.new) or
related APIs will perform the entire compilation step synchronously. When
finished no further compilation will happen at runtime or later during
execution of WebAssembly instances for example.

Compilation of WebAssembly by default goes through Cranelift and is recommended to be done once-per-module. The same WebAssembly binary need not be compiled multiple times and can instead used an embedder-cached result of the first call.

`Module` is thread-safe and safe to share across threads.

[§](https://docs.rs#modules-and-clone)Modules and `Clone`

Using `clone` on a `Module` is a cheap operation. It will not create an
entirely new module, but rather just a new reference to the existing module.
In other words it’s a shallow copy, not a deep copy.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

There are a number of ways you can create a `Module`, for example pulling
the bytes from a number of locations. One example is loading a module from
the filesystem:

```
let engine = Engine::default();
let module = Module::from_file(&engine, "path/to/foo.wasm")?;
```
You can also load the wasm text format if more convenient too:

```
let engine = Engine::default();
// Now we're using the WebAssembly text extension: `.wat`!
let module = Module::from_file(&engine, "path/to/foo.wat")?;
```
And if you’ve already got the bytes in-memory you can use the
[ Module::new](https://docs.rs/struct.Module.html#method.new) constructor:

```
let engine = Engine::default();
let module = Module::new(&engine, &wasm_bytes)?;
// It also works with the text format!
let module = Module::new(&engine, "(module (func))")?;
```
Serializing and deserializing a module looks like:

```
let engine = Engine::default();
let module = Module::new(&engine, &wasm_bytes)?;
let module_bytes = module.serialize()?;
// ... can save `module_bytes` to disk or other storage ...
// recreate the module from the serialized bytes. For the `unsafe` bits
// see the documentation of `deserialize`.
let module = unsafe { Module::deserialize(&engine, &module_bytes)? };
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasmtime/runtime/module.rs.html#247-251)**crate features **`cranelift` or `winch` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasmtime/runtime/module.rs.html#247-251)

**crate features**only.

`cranelift` or `winch`Creates a new WebAssembly `Module` from the given in-memory `bytes`.

The `bytes` provided must be in one of the following formats:

- A [binary-encoded](https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/binary/index.html)WebAssembly module. This is always supported.
- A [text-encoded](https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/text/index.html)instance of the WebAssembly text format. This is only supported when the`wat`feature of this crate is enabled. If this is supplied then the text format will be parsed before validation. Note that the`wat`feature is enabled by default.

The data for the wasm module must be loaded in-memory if it’s present elsewhere, for example on disk. This requires that the entire binary is loaded into memory all at once, this API does not support streaming compilation of a module.

The WebAssembly binary will be decoded and validated. It will also be
compiled according to the configuration of the provided `engine`.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

This function may fail and return an error. Errors may include situations such as:

- The binary provided could not be decoded because it’s not a valid WebAssembly binary
- The WebAssembly binary may not validate (e.g. contains type errors)
- Implementation-specific limits were exceeded with a valid binary (for example too many locals)
- The wasm binary may use features that are not enabled in the
configuration of `engine`
- If the `wat`feature is enabled and the input is text, then it may be rejected if it fails to parse.

The error returned should contain full information about why module creation failed if one is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

The `new` function can be invoked with a in-memory array of bytes:

`let module = Module::new(&engine, &wasm_bytes)?;`Or you can also pass in a string to be parsed as the wasm text format:

[§](https://docs.rs#unsafety-1)Unsafety

This function is marked as `unsafe` because if fed invalid input or used
improperly this could lead to memory safety vulnerabilities. This method
should not, for example, be exposed to arbitrary user input.

The structure of the binary blob read here is only lightly validated
internally in `wasmtime`. This is intended to be an efficient
“rehydration” for a [ Module](https://docs.rs/struct.Module.html) which has very few runtime checks beyond
deserialization. Arbitrary input could, for example, replace valid
compiled code with any other valid compiled code, meaning that this can
trivially be used to execute arbitrary code otherwise.

For these reasons this function is `unsafe`. This function is only
designed to receive the previous input from [ Module::serialize](https://docs.rs/struct.Module.html#method.serialize) and

[. If the exact output of those functions (unmodified) is passed to this function then calls to this function can be considered safe. It is the caller’s responsibility to provide the guarantee that only previously-serialized bytes are being passed in here.](https://docs.rs/struct.Engine.html#method.precompile_module)

`Engine::precompile_module`Note that this function is designed to be safe receiving output from
*any* compiled version of `wasmtime` itself. This means that it is safe
to feed output from older versions of Wasmtime into this function, in
addition to newer versions of wasmtime (from the future!). These inputs
will deterministically and safely produce an `Err`. This function only
successfully accepts inputs from the same version of `wasmtime`, but the
safety guarantee only applies to externally-defined blobs of bytes, not
those defined by any version of wasmtime. (this means that if you cache
blobs across versions of wasmtime you can be safely guaranteed that
future versions of wasmtime will reject old cache entries).

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

memory allocation fails. See the

`OutOfMemory` type’s documentation for
details on Wasmtime’s out-of-memory handling.In-place deserialization of an in-memory compiled module previously
created with [ Module::serialize](https://docs.rs/struct.Module.html#method.serialize) or
